title: Shifting Project Requirements? Stay Flexible Without Losing It
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni, who coaches technical professionals on empathy, offers advice for staying effective when project requirements keep shifting. She argues that people should not assume everyone shares the same understanding of methodologies like Agile, and that a requests loop must eventually close without cutting off stakeholder input too early. Her tactics are to listen openly, recap decisions in writing, log requests, and book follow-up sessions before leaving a meeting rather than waiting through stakeholder silence. She distinguishes real calm from dismissiveness, urging cognitive empathy that shows care in tone and eye contact. She reframes changing requirements as organic, normal project life rather than chaos, and sums up the stance as adapt, align, communicate, stay curious and stay calm.
points: Shifting requirements are normal project life, and reframing them as organic rather than chaotic is the first step to handling them well.
Do not assume stakeholders share your definition of Agile or other methodologies; recap in writing and keep a decision log.
Schedule follow-up sessions before leaving a meeting, because silence from busy stakeholders can stall a project for weeks.
Calm only works when it is paired with visible care; cognitive empathy lets a leader reassure without necessarily agreeing.
When you are the tense one, step away before sending an angry email.
quotes: It's a mistake to assume that new or conflicting demands are chaos. Change your perception. They're organic, like the tomato plant overgrowing in my backyard.
The loop has to close at some point. The challenge here is to be patient. Cutting off the input of requirements immediately will result in a non-viable product.
A good practice? Recap what was talked about in writing. Document what was decided in a log. Use this to help remember everything asked so things do not keep popping up.
When things sit too long, they get delayed. You have to remember that stakeholders do not know your timetable or the requirements you need; you do. Take charge of the situation.
It does not require that you necessarily agree with the other tense individual. You can think through though what they are thinking. You can ask questions that are open-ended.
Be the calm one who really listens, documents, and asks questions. People love to talk, so do less of the talking yourself. Take deep breaths, pause before responding, and remain curious.
